samples.summary: Drift is fixed by a source-scraping test rather than by construction; the browser entry could simply re-export the Node entry's helper block
samples.evidence: Both `src/index.ts:75-89` and `src/node.ts:101-115` hand-maintain the identical block-helpers export list, and the new test (`test/store/entry-parity.test.ts`) enforces the invariant by regex-parsing the two source files. Since the block-helpers module is DOM-free by definition, having the browser entry re-export from the Node entry (or from a single shared `store/block-helpers-exports` barrel) would make drift structurally impossible and remove the need for a text-scraping guard. This is an approach preference, not a failed requirement.

samples.summary: Parity guard covers only `./store/block-helpers.js`, though the two entries duplicate several other export lists that can drift the same way
samples.evidence: `blockHelperExports()` hard-filters on `SOURCE = './store/block-helpers.js'`, so the equally hand-duplicated `model/types.js` (index.ts:~40-70 vs node.ts:58-82) and `model/named-styles.js` (index.ts:55-62 vs node.ts:84-92) blocks remain unguarded. The same failure mode (a symbol added to the browser entry only, breaking `YorkieDocStore` under the Node-resolving integration lane) applies to those modules; scoping the guard to one module leaves the stated risk only partially closed. Also the check is one-directional (browser ⊆ node) by design, which is defensible, but worth stating.
